title: What a PMS is
objectives: Define a PMS and its three types.
State the three numbers to remember: ₹50 lakh, 15 to 30 stocks, own demat.
body_md:
A PMS is a professionally managed portfolio of securities held directly in the client's own demat account, regulated by SEBI, with a minimum investment of ₹50 lakh.

## What a PMS is

- Discretionary: the portfolio manager decides what to buy and sell. This is the most common type.
- Non-discretionary: the manager recommends, but each trade needs the client's approval.
- Advisory: the manager only advises; the client executes.
- Portfolios are concentrated, typically 15–30 stocks, so they can differ sharply from the index, both up and down.
- Since April 2023, every PMS investment approach is grouped under one of four strategies (equity, debt, hybrid, multi-asset) and compared against a common benchmark, with data published through APMI.
example: A client invests ₹60 lakh in a discretionary PMS. A demat account opens in her own name and the manager buys 22 stocks in it. She sees every holding and every trade in her statement.
say: Unlike a mutual fund, the stocks are held directly in your own demat account.
The manager runs a focused portfolio of 15 to 30 stocks, so it can do very differently from the index.
never: PMS is a better mutual fund.

talk_track.title: The PMS Distributor
talk_track.text: Welcome to Module 2 of the Fund Horizon training series: the PMS Distributor. Portfolio Management Services are a concentrated, high-ticket product held in the client's own name. So our job is due diligence and suitability first, and access second. We'll follow the same L.E.A.R.N. framework as Module 1: Learn the basics, Evaluate the client, Act right, Review and rebalance, and Navigate behaviour.

talk_track.title: L.E.A.R.N. applied to PMS
talk_track.text: Here's how L.E.A.R.N. applies to PMS. Learn: what a PMS is, and who is allowed to sell it. Evaluate: the most important idea in this module is that being eligible for PMS is not the same as being suitable for it. Act right: proper due diligence on the strategy, and fees explained in rupees, not percentages. Review: judge a PMS on after-fee returns against its benchmark. And Navigate: concentrated portfolios fall harder, so keeping clients steady matters even more than with mutual funds.

talk_track.title: What a PMS is, in three numbers
talk_track.text: A Portfolio Management Service is a professionally managed portfolio held directly in the client's own demat account, regulated by SEBI. Remember three numbers. Fifty lakh rupees is the SEBI minimum. Fifteen to thirty stocks is a typical portfolio, much more concentrated than a mutual fund. And one demat account in the client's own name, so they can see every stock and every trade. There are three types: discretionary, where the manager decides every trade, and which is the most common; non-discretionary, where the client approves each trade; and advisory, where the manager only advises. Since April 2023, every PMS approach is grouped into one of four strategies, equity, debt, hybrid or multi-asset, and compared against a common benchmark, with data published through APMI.

talk_track.title: Fewer stocks, bigger bets
talk_track.text: Here's why PMS behaves so differently from a mutual fund or an index. The Nifty 50 spreads money across fifty stocks. A typical PMS holds about twenty, so each stock carries far more weight. When the manager is right, that concentration can beat the index by a wide margin. When the manager is wrong, or the style is out of favour, it can lag by a wide margin too. Every PMS client must understand this before they invest: the same concentration that creates the upside creates the downside.

check.q: What is the SEBI minimum investment for a PMS?
check.why: PMS needs ₹50 lakh. AIFs typically need ₹1 crore.

check.q: Where are the securities in a PMS held?
o: In the client's own demat account
check.why: The client owns the shares directly and can see every holding and trade.

check.q: In which type of PMS does the manager decide every trade?
check.why: Discretionary is the most common type. In non-discretionary the client approves each trade; in advisory the manager only advises.
